RELEASE OF MR. CA ItEW, M.P.-
BRUTAL PRISON TREATMENT.

:r One of Mr. Balfour's prisoners. Mr. Carew. M.P.. ! walked into the Dublin " Evening Telegraph " office on Monday afternoon, a free man. A month of hie sentence Was still unexpired. but his dis- charge had been ordered inconsequence of his state of health. Mr. Carew looked blanched and delicate, and in much need of a change of scene. The record I of his weight in h.'ilkenny Gaol on 21 reli. was List. Tlb. When weighed in Kilmainham Prison last I Friday be had deteriorated to lint. 111 b. A 'Telegraph" representative asked Mr. Carew to state ! the exact circumstances relating to the atteinpt to clothe him in prison garb by force, a struggle whWli was mentioned at the time in the newspapers with- out details. It occurred in Kilkenny l'rison on the ' first day. Six warders entered his cell and tore off his clothing, after a determined struggle, Miring which they wrenched his right leg and hurt his left arm. They then endeavoured to force the hon.' member into the prison clothes, but he resisted, anti they failed. Ile was left naked in his cell from that time—Thursday -until the following Monday, 25 Feb. On that date in consequence of the visit of Dr.O'Farrell, medical officer to the Prisons Board, Ida drawers and ve-t were returned. lie remained attired only in these garments until the following Monday. 4th March. The struggle, therefore, extended over eight days, iind was terminated only by Mr. Caren- 's removal in his own clothes to Kil- mainham Prison on 4 March. No attempt was made to deprive him of his clothing during the remainder of his imprisonment. Mr. Carew's release left eight members of Parliament in gaol, but Mr. William O'Brien's release this week reduces the number to seven. _4.--

Answering a question in the House of Commons, 4,11 Monday, he said :—" Her Majesty's Government were fully alive to the great import- ; ance of maintaining the Convention signed by !seven out of the eight great bounty-giving Powers, and accepted in principle by the rightly" If this j be no, it is thee that the people of this country were alive to the importance of getting rid of the • IGovernment. Granted that bounties are unwise in policy on the part of the countries that give them, it does not by any means follow that it is unwise for in to accept the benefit derived from • them. We are having, or rather have been having. sugar from the Continent at artificially low rates: . hut why should we concern ourselves about that ? What if the bounty-givers were se bountoms as to ; send on sugar for nothing—would that be a calamity ? Why cannot we let well alone ? It is I said that the bounties have interfered with the ; growth of sugar refining in this country : indeed j some go no for as ti say they hare thrown men ant ; of work, But if this be no, there has been ample mripensation —not to the individual but to the community. Such is the impetus given to the jam, confectionery, and biscuit industries that ten Inca en have been found work for one reduced to • enforced idleness in connection with the sugar - refiners. And what of these ten ? Are they to I walk the streete in order that the one may ! obtain employment her the Baron's Bill ? If we are to legislate at all, let us in the name of all that is rational legislate to ensure as for as we cam the greatest happiness of the great- eat number. But we contend that in this case legislation can do nothing but harm. It is Pro- tection of the worst possible kind, and in the interest of a ridiculously small number. The ; benefit that is being sought is not that of the unemployed workman, who is simply put forward j as a stalking horse; it is the rich sugar-refiner and the rich planter who desire to grow richer still at the expense of the poor to whom sugar has become al t a necessary of life. If we are tot have Protection, let in have it openly, and let nal ; begin with the farmer, who has had and in still j having a terrible struggle for existence. We do 'not, to be surc,advocate such a course, but it would j he infinitely preferable to the scheme before the country: and it would besides have an honest look ! , with it, Winch is 11191 v than van be Yuitl for the Sugar Convention Bill.

The Month Mu Poets wnte of the promise of May;if but the May we are having is not a May of promise oak, but .of performance. It has burst upon on with the refulgence of sunnier, and it has had such an effect upon vegetatimi that it seems tame to say , you can see things grow; the process is so active 1, that it suggests hearing as well as seeing. At such a time it is a luxury to live—that is, if one is not bothered with duns, or out of health, or over- powered with the heat. There is always an "if " for the law of compensation operates untrewsingly. Still, if the duns are troublesome, what can be better than giving them a long trail out of town l• It will do them and you good to settle accounts, or put them r4l, in the country for one must he in the country to enjoy the luxury of life at this season of the year, when the apple tree looks as sweet as a bride in its blossom of pink mid white ; when the hawthorn is whitening and scenting the hedges ; when cottage gardens are flowery and fragrant; and when gushing birds relieve their overcharged hearts in an ecstasy of song. If one luis lost health, to be amidst ell this is surely the best way of lindieg it ;and, found or not found, existence is more tolerable in I the fresh, green lane than in the smoke-smitten street. And as to the heat even that is softened with the grass under foot, and the branch of mil !oak or an elm overhead. It takes time, to he Imre, , Iffy the towniunan to get out in the country, but it is time well spent. There is no such soother of! !nerve, and bracer of muscle, as a country walk. It puts heart in u man, and Ms him for gray- piing with life's troubles, and trials, and perplexing problems. People too often rush to stimulants when they are exhausted with the day's or the week's work. What they really want is to recreate not to stimulate ; and that is best accomplialied by change of scene and change of air --by wander_ in', if only for an hour at a time, into " fresh woods said pastures new: Man made the town, but God made the country. Why, then, not seek inspiration and renovat at the fountain head? The world is too much with us; late and aeon,

Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers. Ah ! this "getting and spending a worry it is! But if we would lessen the worry—if we would recruit rather than lay waste our powers— we must spend time in the eountry ; with the grass at our feet; with the lark overhead; and the blue sky over all.

and the meeting in London, on Tuesday, P6""'". "g"' under the auspices of the Grand Habitation td the Primrose League,- but it cannot be sa.l that he made a great speech. Ho was surrounded with dames and knights of the League, wearing their jewels And badges,- and yet he woe not wholly happy. Can it be that, genuine aristeerat as he is, and understanding the real thing, he has a lordly contempt for mongrel knights and sham dames It w, mid he worth something to know ',is real thoughts about '• the champion banner," and " the champion habitation of the year lii wonders, it may be, whether he will be r“mired next year, or the year after, to bestow a benison On the champion dame and the eleeopien clo-doncer. Non, Lord DeAcoNermo wouldl have been quite at home at such a Inaction. Ho would hove laoghed in his sleeve at it, but at the same time be wonld have fooled the League to the top of its bent with the gayest of "gay wisdom." Lonl SALISBURY is wise in his way, but lie is not gay Inc does not adapt himself suffi- ciently to the line foolery of the occasion. He was never an admirer of Lord litAvosermo

--at no time he absolutely detested him— and it is not improbable that lie dislikes the fuss which is imode to keep his rival's memory green. It is suggestive, at any rate, that in the course of his address he never once mentioned Lord Bits- Ittial'lLLl;ti name ; nor did he descend to the folly of talking about "die favourite flower." He contented himself, for the most part, with utter- ing vague generalities--of the kind that are dis- tinguish.' for sound rather than sense. For instance, we are told that ...The danger, if danger there is, to the special institutions the League in called upon to defend is I hat, in modern SOCit.tr, the ancient welding toge- ther of all altisaael with each other has been rudely I shatteml and dislocated, the industrial necessities of the time, generation after generation, having gathered the various classes of the country more and more, and greatly too much, in isolated posi- tions. 80 that their mutual influence upon each other in Kitt what it was in old times."

Reduced to I.lain English, what this high-sounding sentenee MOMS is that the democracy is asserting itself, and is not for the future to be led by the nose by the aristocracy. The League is to be called upon to back up "the special institm tions----such its the Church with its wealthy NAP ,ps aid starvling curates; the landowners with their ,de,t4 active and destructive ideas of primo- , geniture, entail, and royalty rents ; and the House of Lords with its mischievous meddling, semi- idiots, and black sheep. Defending these is defending what Lord SALISBURY is pleased to call "vdigicr, and the empire, :ind the institutions of the country in winch we am bore He has no sympathy adh the masses ; he never had, nor is it likely that he ever will have.

" Liberty." be sayo, " is now threatened by the tendency of sections of the community that by some etiat.c.• hat .. got hold r•I a superior power at the ballot or in Parliament. to impose their ideas or to enftree their unjust interests at the expense of the rights and just claims of their fellows.

Oh! that ballot-box ! It has always been is hideous thing to the loader of the Tory ',arty. He fought tooth and nail against working-men being entnisted with the franchise, and he would to-day deprive then, of it if he eudd hut, as he cannot do that, the League is exhorted to protect Liberty by wheedhng the weaker ones into parting with their birthright fora Ihnichof Primroses. He was boand to di, that: hot, with Witmay flitax•es action for libel hangiag over his heel, he sought for once to modlemte" the ralemur of his tongue." He did not protest that Irish Is slurs were thieves and murderers. but he said "They hare formed an alliance with a very widespread feeding, not a very respectable feeling, hut the desire of people to m 0.0814 what belongs to their neighbours. That is dignified usually by the name of • te.,rrarian feelieg. i Laughter.) It is as good a name as any other hut I will find you an ' agrarian feeling in any street in London:. Well, it may lie wrimg for the Irish tenant to try to stick to the hit of land which he has bnaight into culti- vation on the barn hillside hot there is. growing feeling that it is It greater wrong for aristocrats of the SA tr,re sr type to hold land which they do not uititivoti Cu seise property (under expired 'wisest which they have not Isn't and to exact millions a yesr hw the privilege of getting miner- als !ire or ought to he the property of the State. Lord SAM:OOU does well to dread the lem ,if the ballot he dreads it as one who has done ill. There is is day of reeln,ling at hand; and it is not to be oti either IT a crafty Prime !Minister Or /1.1,1111. a. Primrose League.

there has been another licensing appeal before the Court of Queen's Bench. A mandamus had been obtained to compel the justicesof the borough of Congleton to reconsider a case of refusal to I renews license. They did so; they Vdn listened to the voice of the Chief Constable, who 4:‘te4 that ' the house was not wanted; and they again refused to renew. Hence the appeal, which has resulted in favour of the decision of the justices. Chief Constables should take note of this judgment, and act accordingly.

Lady Sandhurst, it will be remembered, was elected a member of the London County Council, but, through a defect in the law, it was found that because size WitS 0 woman she was not qualified to sit. On Monday a bill qualifying women to sit, elected, as Comity Councillors I just 14•1 they can hold scats lin Boards of Guardians, and School Boards), earn,. up for second reading in the House of Lords, and was rejmted by is majority of h 5. The Lords are always in mischief; they are jealous of female qualifications- there are so many old women amongst them.

Mr. Carom, M.P., has been released from gaol before his sodenoo was completed because three months in Kilmainham have nearly killed him. He was brutally stripped of his clothing, and, in'- cause he would not put on the felon's dress, he was left naked in his cell for four days! It is now ad- mitted that there was no need limier the prismi rules to attempt to enforce such a regulation, and I Mr. Carew ought to have some remedy against I Mr. Balfour. If the Trish Secretary Whits deserts, he would he tied to a cart tail and dogged by every Irish M.P. he has tried to degrade. Notwithstanding the higher price for gas at Padgate Schools, it is suggestive of the need for inquiry when it is found that the gam bill for Pad- gate Schools is thl, as against T.2S only for the ! whole of the Workhouse. It seems that " the cost of gas at the Workhouse has lawn redmed from Int to tgls through strictly looking after the consumption." This is greatly to the credit of tke I Workhouse master ; but what cd the waste in the ' past? What would an employer think whew" gnu bill was reduced 0110 half through care being taken? Would he not him, something to say as to previous hick of care % A London correspondent, referring to the recent debate in the House of Commons on perpetual pensions, says Amongst the list of pensk ins in:, ulna one ;standing to the credit of a Scottish pimr I for the fulfilment of a sinecure office. A member lof the House of Commons, bantering the noble lord on this source of revenue, learned the start- ling fact that for two generations not a penny had I gone into the family coffers. His grandfather, I being in need 11f ready money, add the pension to a Portsmouth Jew, whose heirs and assigns draw it Ito this day." This is one of thoBo 1,11111113 of which I Byron said --" His each 0011103 from, his wealth I goes to, a Jew."

div.p: BUILVL El" GAZETTE, Febraary 23rd. GIIE lot of those who toil from day to day in the bowels of the earth is not a very agreeable one. Apart from the terrible risks of which we are so often reminded by a calamitous explosion, _ .

with all its thrilling scenes, the collier has to pursue his work at times under circumstances of great hardship. Mr. Moses Knowles, of 109, Oxford Road, Burnley, has had some experience of the trying conditions of labour in some:of the deeper coal mines of this country. He relates how he has repeatedly had to work for hours crouched in ten or twelve inches of watv and the cold liquid at the same time dropping all over his body from above. Happily such condit of employment are almost unknown in the Burnley district, but Mr. Knowles has lr,,' encounter them in other mining sufferer in consequence. He first commenced with pains in his head, which gradually extended to other parts of the body.' " I got so low," said Mr. Knowles, with blankets and have a chair close to the fire even en a warm day. It was only then that I could feel anything like warmth. My legs got so weak that I had to have the help of a stick to get across the 'floor. I was terribly troubled with indiges- tion, nervous debility, and disease of the liver and kidneys, and had constant attywks of cilimp in the stomach. For many weeks I suffered dreadfully, writhing in agony for hours toether, and got so weak that it was painful to speak, let alone trying to move. Medicine only seemed to make me worse, and I got so that my friends gave Inc up and the doctor ventured to offer no hope of a cure. At last I read one of Warner's pamphlets, sent for a bottle of 'Warner's SAFE Cure,' and oh! how much good it did me. In a few weeks I was a new man. My appetite returned, the weakness disappeared, and I went hack to my work feeling stronger than 1 had done for years."

FOOTBALL.
THERE is a shadow over all civilization! What is it? Whence comes it ? A plain statement of facts must answer these questions. And our words must
be serious—as befits so important a subject. Let us, then, go straight to
the point.
First consider this fact: No man lives his allotted life. Most of as die before
we have begun to learn what it is to live. Longevity is the fortune of but few ; the
great mass die a premature death. The reverse ought to be the ease, and would be, if

div.head: nature and true science could have their way.
div.p: nature and true science could have their way.
The length of life ought to be from five to eight times the duration of the
period of growth.
This is true of all animals. Man's period of growth is about twenty
years, and the average length of his life should be HO years. Indeed, Haller, who
collected a thousand cases of reputed longevity, placed the limit of human life at a little
less than 200 years. What is the appalling conclusion ? This: That all who die
before they are 100 years old, die prematurely.
downhill.
Disguise it as we may, we cannot overlook the truth that the race is going
It is not improving; it is degenerating. Proof of this is everywhere pre-
sent to the man who will open his eyes and look at it. Intellectually and mentally we
see decided progress, but not physically. Our schools and colleges cram young minds
with information and stimulate them to study, then dismiss them in broken health to
Men and women devoid of bodily strength and without vital resistance are the
vast majority of our population. A breath of gentle air, a alight draft coming at an
unguarded moment, is a messenger of evil to every one of them. A change in the
atmosphere gives them neuralgia, or rheumatism, or lets loose the hidden powers of a
wasting consumption. Like hothouse plants, we have to be kept under glass. We
dare not enjoy life lest we lore it!
Is this an overdrawn picture? No; not by a line or a tint. The Shadow is
infinitely deeper, broader, and darker than any pen can sketch it. Every intelligent
person knows this to be so. We all live in daily apprehension from it. We understand
and feel that disease and death lurk in all the places we inhabit and follow our steps
wherever we go. Our fellows and companions are struck down at our side. Yesterday
we talked together, both in average health; to-day one out of two is dumb for ever.
Yesterday we had wife, husband, or child ; to-day the circle is irreparably broken
Insanity is so common as to scarcely excite comment. Institutions for the
care and treatment of the insane are numerous and crowded, and thousands of homes
contain at least one member suffering from some form and degree of insanity—these
unfortunates being a constant source of care, responsibility, and danger to the devoted
household.
Whence does this Shadow arise? The answer is plain. It arises from the
prevalence of indigestion and dyspepsia.
For example, how many there are who suffer from feelings like these: Their
food does not agree with them. They can hardly keep anything on their stomachs—
even the things that are said to be the easiest to digest. They have a sour stomach,
and a sense of fullness and deadness after eating; headache, dizziness, foul breath, and
often lie awake most of the night, and when they do sleep are troubled with bad dreams.
Besides this, they are nervous, restless, and fidgety, and have no ambition for labour or
exertion of any kind.
The mind is weak, too, and it is hard for them to " remember
anything." From time to time they will have palpitation of the heart and difficulty to
breathe, so it seems as if they would suffocate. There is a bad taste in the mouth and
a sort of slime on the teeth, and a dark coat on the middle and back part of the tongue
The nerves are all out of tune, and the least sudden noise or unpleasant news upsets
them and makes them depressed and irritable.
The remedy for this dangerous condition is Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup.
It imparts tone and strength to the weak stomach and bowels, promotes the flow of the
gastric juice, and enables the blood to take the nutritious elements from the food and
convey them to all parts of the body.
Two or three bottles have effected a cure after
the disease had reached an advanced stage, and it nevar fails to act beneficially when
used according to the directions. It expels all foul humours from the system and
restores the energies of health. Resort to Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup at the first
appearance of any of the above symptoms.
Mr. I. H. Evans, Chemist, Lymm, Cheshire, says: "I herewith send you a
testimonial from a person whose wife had long been seriously ill and given up all hopes
of recovery. She is now well, through the use of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup."
Mr. F. J. Neade, Chemist, Terenure Road, Rathgar, writes:
"Mr. Hynes, of
No. 2, Rathgar Square, was ill for a long time from a stomach affection, which neither
myself nor three doctors could relieve. He was completely cured by one bottle of
Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup."
Mr. John MeGavin, Chemist, 110, Friargate, Preston, writes : " On all sides
I hear Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup praised as a remedy for constipation, indigestion,
and dyspepsia, and for liver troubles. We sell it to the same people repeatedly, which
proves how they appreciute it."
Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup is for sale by all chemists and medicine
vendors, and by the proprietors, A. J. White, Limited, 35, Farringdon Road, London,

I should my, roughly judging, that it contains about 25 to 30 square ntiles ; a great part mounkins. DEATH OF AN OLD VOLUNTEER. Last evening Mr. John Jones, builder, died at his reddence, in Nicholson-st., after having been ill for some time. The deceased, who was about 55 years of one, was very well-known in the town, and was one of the oldest members of the local Volunteer corps in which he was a colour-sergeant. lie was also, we believe, a Freemason.

Hitherto Prenot has been renownml for watch movements as a speriality, some of their productions being remark- able for precision, keeping time for years without awistion. REV. THOMAS NIECES, MA. Ile was trained at the DI anebester College. York, was minister at Cork from 1829 to 1.1441, at Eustae, st., Dublin 1841-42. at Warrington 1844-46. Exeter 1846.52. IIEV. PHILIP I'HARBAI.I. CATIFRNTER, 8.A., in 1846. Ile was born at Bristol. November 4th, 1819, , and received his training alsoat Manchester College, York. fie settled first at Stand. near Manchester. 1841, whence he removed for Warrington. During 11l years he ministered to this congregation, o Under his active care: SKS, a writer in these erdumns a year ago, .` new life seemed to spring up in the quiet chapel. A printing press VIM erected by him, and from it came books, pamphlets, hymns, and music of many kinds. Open-air services and temper- ance meetings were held by the indefatigable pastor that attracted half the town ; but his health failed him, and he went fora short time to America, where he received the degree of Or. of Philosophy." On his return, th, unsanitary condition of the chapel necessitated its being altered very considerably. Ile finally resigned in 1869, and went back to Montreal, where he died May 24th, 1877. From his tablet erected in the chapel at Warrington at the Joint expense of many friends," we gather the following estimate of his character : A student of nature, a servant of God and a lover of mankind. As a preacher he was simple, faithful, heartsearching. Au It student untiring, ever learning that he might teach. As a teacher, earnest, loving and beloved. Ills heart glowed with all personal affection, and yearned for an ever closer walk with (Rid. He

div.p: BATHING FATALITY AT W.,•:BRINGTON.

On Thursday afternoon, a youth named Frank McHugh. aged 17. son of Michael McHugh, of Dye- , houses, llowiey quay, was drowned in the riser , Mersey, near Latchfonl locks, while bathing, I Deceased, wits wan a factory ham., was employed 1 at the Florence Mill, and about half past two on Thursday afternoon the mill was stopped for want of water. AcHugh. in company ,vith two othors. named Wm. Chandler and Patrick Kelly, then went to bathe in the river. Deceased and Chandler swam across to the Cheshire side. and on attempting to return demased was seen to he struggling, eight or nine yarns from the bank. Chnadler endeavoured to render him assistance. but was unable to do so, and he sank and was drowned. The body was shortly afterwards recovered by a man named Isaac Sankey. The facts of the Cfltse hare been communi- cated Co the Coroner and an inquest will be held.

THE' FATAL ACCIDENT AT BEWSET FORGE. On Monday, Mr. Brighouse, coroner for South- West Lancashire, held an inquest al the Three lipsaus tnn. Tanners-lane, ou view of the body of Thomas Maloney (45), a ccal heaver, who was killed on the afternoon of the F mei., Thursday, whilst working at Bewsey forge. Ile was moving & truck with a crowbar when an engine thio was coming in an opposite direction struck the buffer of the truck and caused it to turn over. The n.sult was that Maloney was jammed between the waggon and a staek of pig iron, anti, when the engine had been reversed and the truck righted, it was found that he had received serious injuries, to which he !Monty afterwards succumbed. John Garrett and Michael Itellmy, both of whom are employed at the forge, were called as witnesses, and the latter stated that at the time of the accident the deceased was engaged in "pinching' tho wheel alike waggon, which was foul of the main line. it was doubtful whether the engine driver could have observed that circumstance, even if he had been looking out. The driver, Edwin Shoobridge, also gave evidence. Ile depased that he had been employed at Bewsey forgo for over seven months, and that for seven years he had been in the employ as a driver of the London r.nd North-Western Railway Company. When he drove down She main line the first time , the line was clear, and when he Wan coming back he did nee see that a waggon had fouled it.
